title: Education Stinehart, Kevin We Bulldozed the Ecosystem of Childhood Then Blamed Kids for Struggling
author: Stinehart, Kevin
summary: Using an extended metaphor of deer invading his school garden after nearby forests were cleared for development, Stinehart argues that the same dynamic explains children's dysregulation in modern schools: we cleared the natural habitat of childhood and then blamed the children for what they no longer have. The 'habitat' -- empty afternoons for free play, neighborhood packs of kids, small risks, boredom long enough to generate creativity, unsupervised conflict that had to be resolved -- provided children with repetitions in frustration tolerance, social courage, and independence. These were not extras but the ecosystem children need to develop the capacities schools now try to remediate with behavior charts and calming corners. The call to action: restore the forest rather than only build better fences.
points: * Children's dysregulation is an ecosystem problem, not a character problem: the natural habitat of childhood that provided reps in frustration tolerance, social courage, and independence has been systematically cleared. * The 'reps' framework: children used to practice frustration by losing backyard games, practice social courage by entering groups without adult facilitation -- these were developmental work the ecosystem provided for free. * Schools built downstream systems (behavior goals, calming corners, social skills lessons, intervention blocks) to address what the upstream ecosystem was cleared to provide -- downstream remediation cannot replace upstream habitat. * The clearing was not malicious but cumulative: each individual decision (safety, convenience, busy schedules, academic pressure, liability, screens) made sense in the moment. * The right question reframe is from 'what's wrong with kids these days?' to 'what happened to the healthy childhood ecosystem they were supposed to grow in?'
quotes: There is something about a garden that changes children. They notice more. They slow down without being told to slow down. They crouch beside a plant like it has breaking news.
We have cleared away so much of the natural habitat children used to grow inside. Not cruelly. Not usually on purpose. Most of the time, we had reasons that made sense in the moment.
Children got reps with frustration. Reps with conflict. Reps with boredom. Reps with physical challenge. Reps with other kids. Reps with making plans. Reps with having those plans fall apart.
We took away the reps the childhood ecosystem provided. Then we got surprised when children looked underdeveloped. We started lifting the weight for the child each time a struggle came up.

A child falling apart over a pencil may need a calm adult, a boundary, and some direct teaching. But if more and more children are falling apart over more and more ordinary parts of the day, we should probably stop blaming the child.
Those are not extras. They are the forest ecosystem childhood needs to thrive. And a child without enough forest will come looking for what they need.
Maybe it's time to look at the empty landscape and start growing the forest back.
